lead: A cyclic code is a linear block code with one extra promise: shift any codeword one place and you get another codeword. One polynomial, the generator polynomial g(x), then describes the whole code. Encoding becomes multiplication or polynomial division, and the hardware is a short shift register. The CRC that guards an Ethernet frame or a ZIP file is exactly this remainder circuit, and BCH and Reed-Solomon codes are its descendants.
prereq: You need Chapter 7.6 for linear block codes, parity-check matrices and syndromes, plus polynomial long division over GF(2).

blocks.text: A linear block code is cyclic if every cyclic shift of a codeword is also a codeword. Shift the (7,4) word 1101001 one place left and wrap the leading 1 to the right end: you get 1010011, another codeword. That one property lets a single polynomial define the whole code.

Number the bits from the right. The rightmost bit is c₀, the constant term; the leftmost is c₆ in a 7-bit word, in general c_{n−1}. A codeword becomes a polynomial with coefficients in GF(2) — only 0 and 1, added by XOR — so 1101001 is 1 + x³ + x⁵ + x⁶.

blocks.where: c₀ is the rightmost bit of the word, c_{n−1} the leftmost; coefficients are 0 or 1 and addition is XOR.

blocks.text: Multiplying c(x) by x and reducing modulo xⁿ + 1 performs the cyclic shift: over GF(2), xⁿ − 1 and xⁿ + 1 are the same polynomial, so the top bit wraps round to the end.

Linearity means the XOR of two codewords is a codeword. Among the nonzero codewords pick the one of smallest degree; call it the generator polynomial g(x). Every codeword is a multiple of g(x), and g(x) divides xⁿ + 1 exactly. Its degree fixes the code: deg g = n − k, so k = n − deg g.
For the (7,4) code g(x) = x³ + x + 1. Degree 3 gives k = 4, hence 16 codewords. The partner factor is h(x) = (x⁷ + 1)/g(x) = x⁴ + x² + x + 1.

Non-systematic encoding is one multiplication: c(x) = m(x)g(x), with m(x) = m₀ + m₁x + … + m_{k−1}x^(k−1) carrying the k message bits. All 2^k products are distinct codewords, but the message is mixed into the parity, so the decoder must divide before it can read it.

Systematic form keeps the k message bits unchanged in the highest-order positions — the coefficients of x^{n−1} down to x^{n−k}, sent first — and appends the n − k parity bits at the right end, in positions x^{n−k−1} down to x⁰. Division does it in three steps.

items: Shift: multiply m(x) by x^(n−k). The message moves into the high-order positions and n − k zeros appear at the bottom.
Divide x^(n−k)m(x) by g(x) with long division over GF(2). Each subtraction is an XOR; there are no borrows.
Take the remainder b(x), of degree less than n − k, and add it: c(x) = x^(n−k)m(x) + b(x).

blocks.text: c(x) = x^(n−k)m(x) + b(x),  b(x) = [x^(n−k)m(x)] mod g(x)
blocks.where: m(x) is the message polynomial of degree at most k−1; b(x) holds the n−k parity bits; x^(n−k)m(x) means the message shifted left by n−k places.

blocks.text: Adding the remainder cancels it, so c(x) is a multiple of g(x) and hence a codeword. A CRC is this same division read as a checksum.
The parity check polynomial is h(x) = (xⁿ + 1)/g(x), of degree k. A word c(x) is a codeword exactly when c(x)h(x) is a multiple of xⁿ + 1 — the polynomial form of cHᵀ = 0 from Chapter 7.6.

The encoder is a shift register of n − k flip-flops with feedback from the last one, and a gate wherever g(x) has a 1 coefficient. For g(x) = x³ + x + 1 there are three stages R₀R₁R₂, one XOR at the input, and one more between R₀ and R₁, since the x¹ coefficient is 1 and x² is 0.

items: First k = 4 clocks: the message switch is closed, so bits go out to the channel and also into the divider, leftmost bit first.
Next n − k = 3 clocks: the switch opens, the input is held at zero, and the register empties itself out as the parity bits.
The output is the message followed by the remainder: 1101 then 001, giving 1101001.

blocks.text: The syndrome calculator is the same register without the message switch. Clock all n received bits in; the register then holds s(x) = r(x) mod g(x). Zero means no detectable error. Since r(x) = c(x) + e(x) and g(x) divides c(x), the syndrome equals e(x) mod g(x) — it depends on the error alone, not on the codeword sent. That is the heart of syndrome decoding.
The table lists x^i mod g(x) for the (7,4) code. All seven values are different and nonzero, so every single error has its own syndrome and can be corrected.

figure.caption: Systematic encoding of 1101 with g(x) = x³ + x + 1. The shifted message is divided, the remainder 1 becomes parity 001, and the codeword is 1101001; the message bits pass through unchanged.

examples.question: A (7,4) cyclic code uses the generator polynomial g(x) = x³ + x + 1. (a) Encode the message 1101 systematically. (b) The received word differs from a valid codeword by a single error in the x⁴ position; find the syndrome and say what it shows.
steps: Bits are numbered from the right, so the message 1101 with k = 4 is m(x) = x³ + x² + 1.
Shift by n − k = 3: x³m(x) = x⁶ + x⁵ + x³, the 7-bit word 1101000.
x⁶ ÷ x³ = x³; x³·g = x⁶ + x⁴ + x³; XOR leaves x⁵ + x⁴.
x⁵ ÷ x³ = x²; x²·g = x⁵ + x³ + x²; XOR leaves x⁴ + x³ + x².
x⁴ ÷ x³ = x; x·g = x⁴ + x² + x; XOR leaves x³ + x.
x³ ÷ x³ = 1; g = x³ + x + 1; XOR leaves 1. Degree 0 is below 3, so stop. Remainder b(x) = 1, parity bits 001.
c(x) = x⁶ + x⁵ + x³ + 1, so the codeword is 1101001 = 105 in decimal. Dividing it by g(x) leaves 0, which confirms it.
The error is e(x) = x⁴, the third bit from the left of the 7-bit word. s(x) = r(x) mod g(x) = e(x) mod g(x) = x⁴ mod g(x).
x⁴ ÷ x³ = x; x·g = x⁴ + x² + x; XOR leaves x² + x. Degree 2 is below 3, so s(x) = x² + x = 110 = 6 in decimal.
The syndrome is nonzero, so an error is flagged; 110 is the x⁴ entry of the single-error table, so the decoder flips that bit and restores 1101001.
examples.answer: The codeword is 1101001 (parity 001, decimal 105) and the syndrome is 110 (decimal 6), which both detects and locates the error at x⁴.
examples.check:
def poly_mod(a, g):
    dg = g.bit_length() - 1
    while a.bit_length() - 1 >= dg:
        a ^= g << (a.bit_length() - 1 - dg)
    return a

g = 0b1011        # x^3 + x + 1
m = 0b1101        # message 1101
shifted = m << 3  # x^3 m(x) = 1101000
b = poly_mod(shifted, g)
cw = shifted | b
e = 1 << 4        # error at x^4
s = poly_mod(cw ^ e, g)
print(b)
print(cw)
print(s)

traps: Choosing a g(x) that does not divide xⁿ + 1. The code then fails the shift test and is not cyclic.
Attaching the parity bits on the left. Systematic means message in the high-order positions, parity at the right end.
Swapping g(x) and h(x): g(x) has degree n − k and generates the code; h(x) has degree k and checks it.
Borrowing in polynomial subtraction. Over GF(2), addition and subtraction are both XOR; no carries, no borrows.
Reading deg g as k. It is n − k, so k = n − deg g; a (7,4) code needs degree exactly 3.

quiz.q: State the cyclic shift property of a cyclic code, in words and in polynomial form.
quiz.a: Every cyclic shift of a codeword is again a codeword. In polynomials: if c(x) is a codeword, so is x·c(x) mod (xⁿ + 1).

quiz.q: A (15,11) cyclic code has generator polynomial g(x). What is deg g(x), and how many codewords does the code hold?
quiz.a: deg g = n − k = 15 − 11 = 4. The code holds 2¹¹ = 2048 codewords.

quiz.q: Why must the generator polynomial divide xⁿ + 1?
quiz.a: Every shift x^i·g(x) mod (xⁿ + 1) must stay a multiple of g(x). That holds only when g(x) divides xⁿ + 1, so that g(x)h(x) = xⁿ + 1 with h(x) a polynomial.

quiz.q: Encode the message 1010 systematically with g(x) = x³ + x + 1.
quiz.a: m(x) = x³ + x. Shift by x³: x⁶ + x⁴ = 1010000. Division: x⁶ + x⁴ → XOR x³·g leaves x³; x³ → XOR 1·g leaves x + 1. Remainder 011, so the codeword is 1010011.

quiz.q: With g(x) = x³ + x + 1 the received word is 1011001. Find the syndrome and the corrected codeword.
quiz.a: r(x) = x⁶ + x⁴ + x³ + 1. Dividing by g(x) leaves remainder 1, so s = 001. The table gives e(x) = 1 for that syndrome, so flip the last bit: 1011000, which divides exactly by g(x).

quiz.q: Two students encode the same message, one as c(x) = m(x)g(x) and one systematically. Both results are valid codewords. Why are they usually different words?
quiz.a: Multiplying by g(x) mixes message bits across the whole word; the systematic route leaves them in place and appends the remainder. Both are multiples of g(x), so both lie in the same code, but the words coincide only by accident.

quiz.q: A (7,4) cyclic code is proposed with g(x) = x³ + x² + 1. Is this a legal generator polynomial?
quiz.a: Yes. x⁷ + 1 = (x + 1)(x³ + x + 1)(x³ + x² + 1), so it divides x⁷ + 1 and gives a valid (7,4) cyclic code — the other one, whose codewords are the reversals of those from g(x) = x³ + x + 1.

beyond: Not for the exam. The remainder circuit here is sold as a CRC: pick g(x) of degree 16 or 32, clock the frame through, and transmit the final register as the check bits. CRC-32 in Ethernet, ZIP and PNG is exactly this. Cyclic codes are also the root of BCH and Reed-Solomon codes, which choose g(x) with several roots to correct many errors. Good search terms: CRC generator polynomial, shortened cyclic code, systematic encoder LFSR.
